channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Premature screen use can take away play, movement, and face-to-face interaction from young children
item.description: Nearly half of Hungarian children are exposed to screens daily by the age of 18 months, yet what they need most for their development is play, physical activity, face-to-face interactions and active exploration of their surroundings. Early and intensive use of digital devices may pose risks not only because of the time spent in front of screens, but also because it may take time away from these essential experiences.

item.title: How to prepare youth to respond to firearm injury risk
item.description: Firearm injury is the leading cause of death for adolescents in the United States. Most firearm owners prioritize safety, research shows, but strategies aimed at firearm injury prevention among youth have largely focused on policy change instead of teaching them how to identify injury risk.

item.title: Dad's antidepressant use linked to higher metabolic disorder risk in children
item.description: Use of antidepressants by fathers in the months just before pregnancy is associated with a slightly increased risk of metabolic disorders, particularly high blood pressure, in their children, finds a large study from Denmark published by The BMJ.

item.title: ADHD meds in pregnancy not linked to developmental disorders in children
item.description: Children born to mothers who used attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) medication during pregnancy face no increased risk of neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism, ADHD, intellectual disability and learning disorders, finds a large Scandinavian study published by The BMJ.

item.title: Gut microbiome may shape blood sugar benefits of whole grains
item.description: People with prediabetes are at very high risk for developing type 2 diabetes, and improving their diet is one way they can try to fend off advanced disease.

item.title: Heart failure: Advances include earlier detection, treatment options, expert explains
item.description: Heart failure is a common complication of heart conditions; collectively, cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death globally. In heart failure, the heart doesn't pump blood well enough to meet the body's needs, causing a range of symptoms. Jose Nativi Nicolau, M.D., a transplant cardiologist at Mayo Clinic in Florida, describes advances in detection and treatment.

item.title: Genetic information can improve prostate cancer risk assessment
item.description: Genetic information can help provide a more individual assessment of prostate cancer risk among men undergoing PSA testing, according to a new study from Karolinska Institutet published in JAMA Network Open. PSA is a protein produced by the prostate that can be measured with a blood test. An elevated PSA level can be a sign of prostate cancer, but PSA levels can also be affected by other changes in the prostate.

item.title: Membrane developed for dry eye treatment can improve symptoms
item.description: A study led by Aston University's Travé Huarte has shown that a new single six-day treatment for moderate to severe dry eye disease using a modified, windowed amniotic membrane can deliver sustained symptom relief with good treatment compliance.

item.title: Preclinical study suggests corin may help treat deadly brain tumor in infants
item.description: A drug called corin might help treat the most common form of brain cancer in infants, according to a study by Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers. Corin, which was developed at Johns Hopkins Medicine, causes tumor cells to mature into a less aggressive state.

item.title: Novel hormone therapy significantly reduces risk of breast cancer recurrence
item.description: A new type of hormone therapy significantly reduced the risk of invasive breast cancer recurrence or death in patients with early-stage, hormone receptor (HR)-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer compared with standard treatments, according to findings from a large international phase 3 clinical trial co-led by investigators at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

item.title: Youth are turning to AI for mental health support. Here's what families should know
item.description: There are few areas in life where AI isn't shaking things up. And managing mental health is no exception.

item.title: RSV shots safe for older adults, alone or in combo, analysis finds
item.description: Multiple clinical trials have found that respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines are safe in adults. Now, a new study in people age 60 and older shows it's also safe to receive an RSV shot plus another vaccine in the same week.

item.title: Study suggests BMI alone may miss obesity-related dementia risk
item.description: A newer way of defining obesity that looks beyond body mass index (BMI) may identify more older adults with an increased risk of dementia than BMI alone, according to a study published Nov. 25, 2026, in Neurology.

item.title: Same oncogenic mutation, different outcomes: Why some blood vessels develop malformations while others remain resistant
item.description: Why do certain cancer-associated mutations cause malformations in some blood vessels while leaving others largely unaffected? The answer lies in the identity and developmental stage of endothelial cells, the cells lining the inside of blood vessels.

item.title: Creatine is popular with bodybuilders—could it help older adults stay independent?
item.description: Climbing stairs or getting out of a chair can become harder with age, partly because muscle mass and strength tend to decline.

item.title: Date-rape drug GHB disappears within hours, but molecular trace could reveal use two days later
item.description: GHB has long posed a major challenge for the criminal justice system. The substance is eliminated from the body so quickly that proving cases of drugging and drug-facilitated rape can be extremely difficult. Now, researchers at Aarhus University have made a crucial discovery.

item.title: Early-life stress may leave lasting traces in the brain that increase risk of chronic pain
item.description: Researchers from the Heidelberg Faculty of Medicine of Heidelberg University and the Central Institute of Mental Health (ZI) in Mannheim have identified a neural mechanism in female mice through which early-life stress may increase vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety disorders. The findings have been published in the journal Science.

item.title: AI could identify psoriasis and assess its severity from a single photo
item.description: Widely available artificial intelligence models could not only recognize psoriasis from a single photo but also assess its severity, according to an international study by researchers at Semmelweis University. The study, published in Frontiers in Medicine, found that ChatGPT-5 identified the skin condition and correctly assessed its severity with nearly 100% accuracy. However, the researchers caution that, despite the promising results, artificial intelligence cannot replace dermatologists, and anyone experiencing symptoms should seek professional medical advice.

item.title: Alzheimer's drug targets tau protein in promising clinical trial
item.description: An experimental Alzheimer's drug that reduces the production of a protein called tau has slowed the decline in memory and thinking skills by up to 54% in a clinical trial.

item.title: Smoking injures the placenta early in pregnancy, study shows
item.description: It is well known that women who smoke during pregnancy put their unborn babies at risk of being born prematurely or with low birth weight. Tobacco smoke can also injure a growing baby's organs.

item.title: How appreciating nature can make life feel more meaningful
item.description: Spending time outdoors can influence how a person feels, but researchers at Texas A&M University wanted to understand why.

item.title: Teenage girls more in tune with their bodies tend to be happier with how they look
item.description: Teenage girls who are better at recognizing signals from inside their bodies tend to be happier with how they look, according to new research.

item.title: Rare sugar d-sorbose may help control allergic and autoimmune diseases
item.description: Rare sugars are naturally occurring monosaccharides that are scarce in nature and are not readily used by the body as energy sources. Some have physiological effects beyond sweetness, raising interest in their potential health applications. One such sugar, d-sorbose, is a structural relative of d-fructose, but its effects on immune cells have remained unclear. Regulatory T cells (Tregs), identified by the Foxp3 protein, help restrain excessive immune responses and maintain immune balance. Whether a rare sugar can promote these cells has been little explored.

item.title: Patients in Indian clinic were well served by standard WHO-recommended HIV treatment, study finds
item.description: A McGill-led study of HIV patients in Pune, India, who received the tenofovir, lamivudine and dolutegravir (TLD) drug regimen found no improvement in outcomes for those who received versions of the treatment tailored to their personal characteristics.

item.title: Brain organoids in space reveal new clues to Alzheimer's disease
item.description: Researchers at the University of California San Diego have found that spaceflight alters biological processes associated with Alzheimer's disease in different ways depending on genetic background. The study, published on Nov. 25, 2026, in Science Advances, suggests space could reveal changes in brain cells that are difficult to detect on Earth.

item.title: Light-activated nanorobots can boost drug delivery across the blood-brain barrier
item.description: As the primary command center of our bodies, human brains have several layers of protection to help keep them safe from dangerous invaders. Unfortunately, some of these safeguards—in particular, the blood–brain barrier (BBB)—make it hard to deliver medications to this essential organ.

item.title: Mindfulness is linked to better mental health and more beneficial social media use
item.description: Mindfulness is associated with better mental health and with more beneficial patterns of social media use, according to a review published Nov. 25, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Marc Tibber and Charlotte Jones from University College London, United Kingdom.

item.title: Potential limits of breast cancer screening policies across Southeast Asia identified
item.description: In Southeast Asia, breast cancer screening could have limited potential to reduce breast cancer mortality due to screening age eligibility not aligning with the actual ages at which women develop the disease, according to a study by the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine).

item.title: Protein quality control helps regulate circadian rhythms, study suggests
item.description: The body's internal circadian clock helps us feel sleepy at night and wake up in the morning. Using fruit flies, researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have discovered that a cellular quality control process that removes defective proteins during protein synthesis helps regulate the pace of the circadian clock.

item.title: PET/CT imaging provides new insights into type 1 diabetes progression
item.description: A novel molecular imaging approach that measures beta-cell mass in the pancreas can offer valuable insights into the progression of type 1 diabetes, according to new research published in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine. The study found that individuals who have had type 1 diabetes for less than seven years have higher total beta-cell mass and function, larger pancreatic volume and lower intrapancreatic fat compared to those who have had the disease for longer. This valuable information, paired with functional tests, has the potential to significantly improve clinical trials of new therapeutic interventions.
